results.content: # New Study Revisits Laplace Approximation, Validating It as an ‘Effortless’ Method for Bayesian Deep Learning. In the new paper Laplace Redux — Effortless Bayesian Deep Learning, a research team from the University of Cambridge, University of Tübingen, ETH Zurich and DeepMind conducts extensive experiments demonstrating that the Laplace approximation (LA) is a simple and cost-efficient yet competitive approximation method for inference in Bayesian deep learning. This view is challenged in the new paper *Laplace Redux — Effortless Bayesian Deep Learning*, in which a research team from the University of Cambridge, University of Tübingen, ETH Zurich and DeepMind conducts extensive experiments that demonstrate the Laplace approximation (LA) can be a simple and cost-efficient yet competitive approximation method for inference in Bayesian deep learning. Laplace approximation (LA) is classic and simple method for obtaining an approximate posterior inference in deep NNs. Machine learning researchers however have tended to prefer alternative approaches such as variational Bayes or deep ensembles, assuming LA is too costly due to its Hessian computation requirements or that it yields inferior results.

results.title: Sparse subnetwork inference for neural network epistemic uncertainty estimation with improved Hessian approximation | APL Machine Learning | AIP Publishing
results.content: Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of this method, whereas qualitative experiments highlight the impact of Hessian approximation granularity and parameter space utilization in Bayesian inference on mitigating overconfidence in predictions and obtaining high-quality uncertainty estimates. The Laplace approximation (LA), a practical and cost-effective Bayesian learning method, models the local posterior as a multivariate normal distribution (MND) centered at a maximum, with a covariance matrix aligned to local curvature.5 This offers two key advantages: (1) the local maximum is easily obtained through the standard maximum *a posteriori* (MAP) training of neural networks (NNs), and (2) despite quadratic space complexity of the covariance matrix with respect to the number of parameters, accurate and cost-effective curvature estimation is achievable through recent advancements in second-order optimization and precise Hessian approximations.6. Due to the substantial overparameterization of DNNs, preserving their accuracy can be achieved by leveraging a compact subnetwork.7 Similarly, accurate predictive posteriors for the entire model can be obtained by performing inference on a reduced subset of model weights.8 However, common approximations to the Hessian matrix (i.e., the inverse of the covariance matrix), such as the Generalized Gaussian–Newton (GGN) and Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), are consistent with the Hessian matrix only under two conditions: (1) when the network is a perfect predictor and (2) when the network is linear.9 Consequently, the Hessian coincides with GGN and FIM for the last layer of the DNN, which is typically linear.10 This motivates the utilization of LA solely on the final layer of the neural network, ensuring precise Hessian estimation and cost-effective representation of uncertainty. Drawing on the preceding discussions, we have developed a last-layer Laplace approximation with low-rank corrected Kronecker-factored curvature approximation, denoted as LLLA-LR-C, for epistemic uncertainty estimation in neural networks. 1. A novel last-layer Laplace approximation with low-rank corrected Kronecker-factored curvature approximation method, denoted as LLLA-LR-CKFAC, is introduced for epistemic uncertainty estimation in neural networks. In this work, we introduce a neural network uncertainty estimation method that utilizes a Kronecker-structure-preserving low-rank representation of the Hessian matrix and the last-layer Laplace approximation.
